chapter_en: Between a Person and His Fellow

sections.title_en: 1. Love Your Fellow as Yourself
sections.body_en:
Rabbi Akiva said: "'And you shall love your fellow as yourself' – this is a great principle in the Torah" (Vayikra 19:18; Sifra there; Jerusalem Talmud Nedarim 9:4). And it is fitting to ask: why did Rabbi Akiva choose precisely this mitzva out of all the other mitzvot in the Torah, so that about it alone he said, "This is a great principle in the Torah"? Is the mitzva of Shabbat not more important than it? And are the mitzvot of tallit and tefillin not as important as it? What is the great principle folded into the mitzva of "love your fellow as yourself", that out of all the mitzvot Rabbi Akiva chose it and said that it is a great principle in the Torah?

The simple explanation says that all the mitzvot between a person and his fellow are in practice included under the mitzva "And you shall love your fellow as yourself". And since most of the mitzvot a person encounters in his life deal with matters between a person and his fellow, it turns out that "And you shall love your fellow as yourself" is the great principle in the Torah, which is the foundation for their fulfilment (Rashi, Shabbat 31a). We will mention here only some of the Torah's mitzvot between a person and his fellow: the prohibition of lashon ha-ra and rekhilut, do not take revenge and do not bear a grudge, the mitzva to lend money to the poor, the mitzva of tzedaka, visiting the sick, rising before the elderly, all the mitzvot dealing with the order of judgement and with the laws of punishments and monetary matters – and these, as said, are only examples.

Moreover, there is a fundamental difference between the mitzvot between a person and his fellow and the other practical mitzvot in the Torah. There are many mitzvot that one can fulfil without any intention; for example, one can keep kashrut and Shabbat without any intention or special attitude. But the mitzvot between a person and his fellow cannot be fulfilled without love. How, for example, would tzedaka that a person gives without love look? Or what meaning would there be to visiting the sick done as a rote commandment of men, without a personal attitude towards the sick person? And therefore Rabbi Akiva said: "'And you shall love your fellow as yourself' – this is a great principle in the Torah", for without it very many mitzvot cannot be fulfilled.

sections.title_en: 2. A Further Explanation
sections.body_en:
However, there is room to add and explain that not only the mitzvot between a person and his fellow depend on the mitzva of love of one's fellow, but even the mitzvot between a person and God depend on it. This is in fact the main innovation in the words of Rabbi Akiva: that all the mitzvot depend on love of people, beginning with the mitzvot between a person and his fellow and ending with the mitzvot between a person and God (Maharal, Netivot Olam, Netiv Ahavat Ha-Re'a, ch. 1).

A person who does not love his friends, his brothers, the members of his people, will never be able to believe in God, and consequently will not be able to fulfil any mitzva as it should be. A person who does not love his fellows is a selfish person, closed up within himself and concerned only with his desires and his private needs; and such a person is not capable of raising his eyes and asking who created the world, the heavens and the earth. For one who does not love his friends is not at all interested in creation; he is interested in the world only in order to use it for his private needs, but the world in itself does not interest him, and consequently the Creator of the world does not interest him either.

The breakthrough out of narrow egoism into the expanses of faith is made through love. Without love the whole world shrinks into the small bubble of selfishness, in which there is no room at all for spiritual ideals. Only a person who knows what love is is capable of understanding what faith is. And love is not a mere word, but a psychological reality in which a person identifies with another, until he loves him as he loves himself. And through this his selfish and petty framework is broken through, and he begins to look at the world as it truly is, and out of this faith is revealed. Therefore Rabbi Akiva said: "'And you shall love your fellow as yourself' – this is a great principle in the Torah."

Now we can also understand the famous saying of Rav Kook: through the sin of baseless hatred the Temple was destroyed, and through baseless love it will be rebuilt. Out of baseless love, a person goes out of his narrow private framework to a broader, more general worldview, and out of this the world will be worthy of the general revelation of the Shekhina of the Temple.

sections.title_en: 3. Love Your Fellow – How?
sections.body_en:
After we have learned about the enormous centrality of the mitzva "And you shall love your fellow as yourself" (Vayikra 19:18), the question arises: how can one fulfil this mitzva? For it sometimes happens that we do not love a certain person or a certain group of people, and there can be many reasons for this – a different character, different opinions, an old insult and the like. And in general, how can the Torah command about matters of the heart? Seemingly it appears that the heart cannot accept any command: if it loves, well and good; and if not, seemingly, the command will not help. Many couples would like the love between them to remain at the same intensity throughout their lives, but the heart, which is what determines these matters, does not agree. Love loses height, gradually diminishes, and it seems that there is nothing to be done. If so, how does the Torah command us to love – or in other words, is the heart at all capable of fulfilling this command?

Many sages explained that the command "And you shall love your fellow as yourself" is not external, but rather addresses something that a person in essence wants. Every Jew in essence loves his brother, for at the root of the soul all are united. However, this love is hidden in the depth of the heart, and the Torah guides us to reveal this love to ourselves and to others.

And what if there is a person towards whom, despite all the beautiful ideas, you do not succeed in revealing the hidden love? For this too there is a solution according to the Torah: do acts of kindness with that person whom you do not love, help him, judge him favourably. If you see him collapsing under his burden, assist him. And then you will discover within your heart that you truly love him. Therefore the Torah does not make do with an abstract command to love, but adds practical mitzvot, such as tzedaka and gemilut ḥesed, through which the hidden love can break through all the barriers and be revealed.

sections.title_en: 4. The Prohibition of Hatred
sections.body_en:
It is a Torah mitzva not to hate a person of Israel, as it is said (Vayikra 19:17): "You shall not hate your brother in your heart." And this does not speak merely of baseless hatred; rather, even a person whose fellow insulted him severely is forbidden according to the Torah to hate the one who insulted him. And this is the language of the Rambam (Laws of Character Traits 6:5): "Whoever hates one of Israel in his heart transgresses a negative commandment, as it is said: 'You shall not hate your brother in your heart.'"

And one must ask: how is it possible to command not to hate even in the heart? For sometimes a person is hurt to the depths of his soul; the insult he has absorbed penetrates and pierces his heart; for whole days he carries his pain – and how is it possible that he should not bear a grudge even in his heart?

In answer to this we will bring a further halakha from the Rambam (Laws of Character Traits 6:6): "When a person sins against another, he should not hate him and keep silent, as it is said about the wicked (II Shmuel 13:22): 'And Avshalom spoke to Amnon neither bad nor good, for Avshalom hated Amnon' (and in the end he killed him by deceit). Rather, it is a mitzva upon him to inform him and say to him: Why did you do such and such to me, and why did you sin against me in such a matter? As it is said (Vayikra 19:17): 'You shall surely rebuke your fellow.' And if he returned and asked him to forgive him, he must forgive…"

In other words: one must talk things over, clarify together every problem and every feeling of unpleasantness. Unlike the false etiquette that says that even if you have a grievance against your friend, do not tell it to him, but hide your hatred in your heart. According to that etiquette it is not dignified for a person to show that he has been insulted, and therefore the first task of one who has been insulted is to hide that insult and wait for the opportune moment in which he will be able to take revenge in a dignified manner… In contrast to this distorted etiquette, which the Rambam calls the custom of the wicked, a person should behave with uprightness and not hide his insult, and come to his fellow and tell him in what way he hurt and insulted him. The Torah believes that every problem between a person and his fellow can be solved through dialogue based on mutual trust. And therefore the mitzva not to hate is joined to the mitzva to rebuke one's fellow, as it is said (Vayikra 19:17): "You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him." And out of people being upright with one another, they will not need to take revenge and bear grudges, and they will be able to love their fellows, as is said in the next verse (there 19:18): "You shall not take vengeance nor bear any grudge against the children of your people, but you shall love your fellow as yourself; I am the Lord."

sections.title_en: 5. The Attitude to a Wicked Person
sections.body_en:
But concerning one who is wicked, the Sages said (Pesaḥim 113b) that it is a mitzva to hate him, for the prohibition of hating is towards your brother, that is, one who is with you in the mitzvot, as it is said (Vayikra 19:17): "You shall not hate your brother in your heart"; but towards one who is not with you in the mitzvot there is no prohibition of hatred. And from where did we learn that it is a mitzva to hate a wicked person? As it is said (Mishlei 8:13): "The fear of the Lord is to hate evil; pride and arrogance and the evil way and the perverse mouth do I hate." And likewise it is said (Tehillim 139:21-22): "Do I not hate them, O Lord, that hate You? And do I not strive with those that rise up against You? I hate them with utmost hatred; I count them my enemies."

And there are two reasons for this hatred: first, the evil of his deeds causes an inner revolt against him. Second, in order to express protest against his evil deeds, and perhaps this protest will rouse him to repent, and at the least it will prevent others from going in his ways.

There are broad discussions about defining the wicked person today, but one can say as a rule that in the mitzvot between a person and God, the wicked person is the one who transgresses in order to provoke. That is, he does not desecrate Shabbat because he does not understand the meaning of Shabbat and it is convenient for him to do melakhot, but he desecrates Shabbat in order to defy and to show that he does not believe in God and His Torah, and he takes no account of the customs of Israel. Whereas in the mitzvot between a person and his fellow, the wicked person is the one who in principle and systematically harms people, and even after they have remarked to him about it, he did not accept it but continues in his evil ways. But one who from time to time stumbles in sins between a person and his fellow is not considered a wicked person whom it is permitted to hate.

And even the wicked person whom it is a mitzva to hate, it is also a mitzva to love, for he is a Jew, and his soul is holy; and an Israelite, even though he has sinned, is called an Israelite (Sanhedrin 44a). And even the wicked who have acted wickedly and corruptly are still called children of God – indeed corrupt children, but children (as in the words of R. Meir in Kiddushin 36a). Therefore the hatred is directed towards the personality that is revealed to us, but the inner essence of every Jew one must love, and hope and pray for him that he will repent (Tanya ch. 32; Middot Ha-Re'aya, Ahava 8-9, and see there 5-6).[1]

notes_en.en: This topic is complex. See Tosafot Pesaḥim 113b; Rambam, Laws of the Murderer 13:13-14; SA ḤM 272:11; Hagahot Maimoniyot on the Laws of Character Traits 6:3; Ḥafetz Ḥayim 4:4, note 14; Ḥazon Ish YD end of siman 2. And see the book "Bein Adam La-Ḥavero" I, pp. 200-272, and the book "Le-Re'akha Kamokha", the mitzva "Lo Tisna", ch. 4. And although the details are very many, it seems that the summary above includes briefly most of the views. And the books of Ḥasidut, foremost among them the books of Rabbi Tzadok Ha-Kohen of Lublin, are full of many sources and deep explanations about the inner virtue and holiness of the transgressors of Israel.

sections.title_en: 6. Do Not Take Revenge and Do Not Bear a Grudge
sections.body_en:
As a complement to the mitzva not to hate a person of Israel, the Torah added two further prohibitions: one, 'do not take revenge', and the second, 'do not bear a grudge', as it is said (Vayikra 19:18): "You shall not take vengeance nor bear any grudge against the children of your people" (Sefer Ha-Ḥinukh, mitzvot 241 and 242).

So that the difference between the two prohibitions may be well understood, we will explain them by way of a story, as explained in the Talmud, tractate Yoma (23a).

Reuven asked Shimon to lend him a hammer, but Shimon did not agree to lend it to him. Of course Shimon behaved improperly, and in his refusal to lend Reuven the hammer he nullified a Torah mitzva, but that is another matter. The next day Shimon – the very one who only yesterday refused to help Reuven – needed to borrow a screwdriver; he came to Reuven and asked him to lend him his screwdriver. And here Reuven faces the question of what to do: whether to take revenge and bear a grudge over what happened yesterday, when Shimon did not want to lend him the hammer, or to ignore it and lend Shimon what he asked for with a pleasant countenance.

According to the Torah, Reuven must wipe the anger out of his heart and lend Shimon the screwdriver with a pleasant countenance. And if Reuven answers Shimon, "I do not want to lend to you, just as you did not lend to me", he transgresses thereby the prohibition "You shall not take vengeance". And if he answers Shimon, "Here is the screwdriver", but adds a mocking jab concerning what happened yesterday, he transgresses thereby the prohibition "nor bear any grudge". And there is no precise wording with which specifically one transgresses "nor bear any grudge"; rather, any kind of mockery connected to what happened yesterday is forbidden. For example, one must not say: "See that I do not behave like you – you did not lend to me when I asked, whereas I am lending to you."

Rather, what must Reuven do? Wipe the hatred out of his heart. For even if he gives the screwdriver without any addition of mockery, and only within his heart bears a grudge against his fellow, in this too he transgresses "nor bear any grudge". All the more so since it is almost impossible that the grudge in the heart will not find expression, whether in words or at least in a look or a tone of displeasure, and from this too Shimon will certainly be hurt.

One must add that it is certainly permitted for Reuven to have a serious conversation with Shimon in order to clarify honestly what the reason was for which Shimon refused to lend the hammer – whether there was here an expression of a negative attitude in principle towards him, or perhaps it was only by chance that Shimon intended to use the hammer at that very time, and for this reason did not want to lend it. That is, to speak seriously at a suitable time in which things can be clarified calmly is certainly good; but it is forbidden to take revenge or to bear a grudge by an expression of mockery.

Of course, in order to fulfil the guidance of the Torah and neither take revenge nor bear a grudge, much strength of soul is needed. But together with this, it should be noted that a person who succeeds in not taking revenge and not bearing a grudge is a happy person; his heart is good, his love of people is firm, and it does not depend on anything.

sections.title_en: 7. Stopping the Quarrel
sections.body_en:
In the Torah prohibition "You shall not take vengeance nor bear any grudge" (Vayikra 19:18), the Torah establishes that there is no place for any quarrel and strife between a person and his fellow, and if by chance some quarrel developed, one must stop it. And even if one side behaves improperly, an obligation is placed on the other side not to take revenge and not even to bear a grudge.

If we succeed in behaving as the Torah guides us, and neither take revenge nor bear a grudge, most of the quarrels between decent people will stop, for generally a quarrel can continue only when there are two sides to it; and the Torah guides each of us that he personally should not cooperate and not pay back his fellow in kind, and thus the snowball will be stopped at the beginning of its path, while it is still small.

But there is still a need to understand more fully the Torah's prohibition to hate, to take revenge and to bear a grudge. For after all, this is a feeling implanted in a person: when he is hurt deeply he is hurt and angry, and wants to pay back the one who hates him in kind. Does the Torah want us to seal our hearts completely, so that we do not feel at all when we are hurt, and thus also not hate? Surely the Torah did not come to nullify feeling, but to direct it and guide it?

In the Jerusalem Talmud (Nedarim 9:4) a fundamental answer to this question is brought. The Yerushalmi says: a person who was walking along the way, and his foot struck a stone, and he fell, and his hand was injured – would it occur to us that the hand, in its great anger, would wish to take revenge on the foot, take a heavy hammer and strike the foot with great force as a punishment for having caused the injury to the hand? And so the Yerushalmi says: all Israel are like one great soul divided into different limbs, and if one limb, one person, harmed his fellow, it is not logical that his fellow should pay him back. It is true that his fellow really behaved towards him in an ugly way, but if he pays him back in kind, only more pain and sorrow will be added – both the hand and the foot will be injured, both he and his fellow will be insulted, and what will come of it? Therefore the Torah guides us: "You shall not take vengeance nor bear any grudge against the children of your people" (Vayikra 19:18), and "You shall not hate your brother in your heart" (Vayikra 19:17).

It is clear that it is very hard to fulfil this mitzva, but together with this the benefit that will grow from keeping these mitzvot is also clear. And not only will society gain from it, but even that person who refrains from revenge and grudge-bearing will in the end profit: he will have fewer enemies, his life will be more pleasant. He will acquire for himself the trait of humility, he will learn to look at the world with a good eye, he will be happy and will live long, and his strengths will be free for developing his special talents and completing his destiny in life.

sections.title_en: 8. To Talk or to Forgive, and Not to Hate
sections.body_en:
According to what we have learned (above, 4), a person who has been insulted or hurt by his fellow has only two paths before him: one, to talk with his fellow in order to correct what is wrong, and this of course is the preferred path. But when it appears that it is not possible to settle the difficulties with the fellow, the second path remains, namely, to wipe the insult and the hatred completely out of the heart. As the Rambam wrote (Laws of Character Traits 6:9): "One whose fellow sinned against him, and he did not want to rebuke him or to say anything to him, because the sinner was very simple or his mind was disturbed, and he forgave him in his heart and did not hate him or rebuke him – this is the trait of the pious; the Torah was particular only about hatred." That is, when there is no chance of a good solution by way of talking things over in peace and friendship, a person is permitted to wipe the hatred out of his heart and forget the matter.

And one must know that when the Rambam explains the reason for refraining from the substantive conversation, "because the sinner was very simple or his mind was disturbed", the intention is not to someone insane in the usual sense; rather, according to the Rambam, even a person who in general is considered normal, if in the area of human relations he is the type who harms his fellow and is not willing to understand the people who were insulted by him, then in this case he is simple and his mind is disturbed.

sections.title_en: 9. In Righteousness Shall You Judge Your Fellow – Judge Your Friend Favourably
sections.body_en:
Among the Torah's mitzvot dealing with relations between a person and his fellow there is a central mitzva: "In righteousness shall you judge your fellow" (Vayikra 19:15). And the Sages explained that the intention is to judge one's fellow favourably (Shevu'ot 30a). As they said in the mishna in tractate Avot (1:6): "Judge every person favourably." And the meaning is that one who sees his fellow doing something that can be interpreted positively and can be interpreted negatively is commanded to interpret it positively. And likewise one who hears a story about his fellow that can be interpreted positively or negatively is commanded to interpret it positively.

To every act that a person does one can give several meanings: one can interpret it positively and find in it the beautiful aspects and the good intentions, and one can also find the opposite. Even to the act of the most righteous person one can give a negative interpretation. Indeed, even the deeds of Moshe our teacher, peace be upon him, Koraḥ interpreted negatively, and thought that his whole intention was to lord it over the people. Let us take for example a person who takes care of his elderly parents. One can say about him: how beautifully he honours his parents; and one can also say: of course he takes good care of them – he is interested in the inheritance…

Regarding all this the Torah instructs: "In righteousness shall you judge your fellow." There is no ignoring here of the negative aspects and the bad intentions that exist; rather, there is an emphasis here on the good and the positive. In almost every act there are both good and bad intentions; the question is what is the main thing, the good or the bad, and the Torah says that the good is the main thing. Every person in his soul, in his inner being, is good, and in his outward aspect he is less good; and the question is what is the main thing – the soul, the inner being, or the outward aspect. By judging his fellow favourably, a person determines that the pure soul is the essence of the person.

sections.title_en: 10. The Details of the Halakha: When It Is a Mitzva to Judge Favourably
sections.body_en:
As we have learned, when an act can logically be interpreted in a good direction or a bad direction, it is a mitzva to interpret it positively, as it is said (Vayikra 19:15): "In righteousness shall you judge your fellow." But when the act appears bad, and according to logic it is hard to interpret it positively, there is no obligation to judge it favourably. And all this is said about a person one knows to be average, neither especially righteous nor wicked.

But if one is speaking of a person who is God-fearing and careful in his deeds, then even if he did an act that on its face appears to be a bad act, as long as it can be interpreted positively – even if for this one needs to give a forced explanation – since one is speaking of a good and righteous person, it is reasonable that the act is not bad as it appears, and it is a mitzva to judge him favourably. And if one judged the righteous person unfavourably, about him the Sages said (Shabbat 97a): "One who suspects the innocent is stricken in his body."

And likewise several incidents are brought in the Talmud (Shabbat 127b) that at first glance appeared very bad, but that person who saw these acts overcame his inclination and interpreted them positively, even though his interpretation seemed seemingly illogical, and in the end it became clear that his positive interpretation was indeed correct. And about him the Sages said that in the merit of having judged his fellow favourably, in heaven too they will judge him favourably.

And the more righteous a person is, the more one must make an effort to judge him favourably. And for this Miriam the prophetess, peace be upon her, was punished, for she did not judge Moshe our teacher, peace be upon him, favourably (Bamidbar 12:1-16).

By contrast, when one is speaking of a wicked person, since his main aim is to do evil, even when one can interpret his deeds for the good, it is right to interpret them for the bad, for presumably that is his intention. And about him it is said (Mishlei 26:25): "When he speaks fair, believe him not, for there are seven abominations in his heart" (Rambam, Sefer Ha-Mitzvot 177, and in the Commentary on the Mishnah, Avot 1:6; Sha'arei Teshuva 3:218; Ḥafetz Ḥayim, positive commandment 3).

But one must be very careful not to determine out of hatred that a certain person is wicked and that consequently one must judge him unfavourably. And so as not to stumble in this, one must strengthen oneself in the mitzva "And you shall love your fellow as yourself" (Vayikra 19:18) and in the mitzva "You shall not hate your brother in your heart" (Vayikra 19:17).

So that the matter may be understood, I will bring an example from our political life here in the Land: one can say that all the people of the left want is to uproot settlements and give parts of the Land of Israel to the Arabs – in short, they are for the Arabs and against the Jews. But one can also say that they are interested in peace and security, and out of genuine concern for the State of Israel they have reached the conclusion that, having no choice, one must give up parts of the Land of Israel. Or that according to their understanding, Jews should not rule over members of another people against their will. Of course one can disagree with their words, but since one is speaking of decent people, one must not judge them unfavourably and give a negative interpretation to their intentions. However, concerning those who behave wickedly, give encouragement to murder organisations, spread slander about the settlers and abandon their blood, it is forbidden to plead in their favour.

sections.title_en: 11. Lashon Ha-Ra
sections.body_en:
The prohibition that perhaps expresses more than anything the proper relations that should prevail between a person and his fellow according to the Torah is the prohibition of lashon ha-ra (evil speech). The centrality of this prohibition is so great that many times the concept of baseless hatred parallels the prohibition of lashon ha-ra. For our Sages of blessed memory said that the prohibition of lashon ha-ra is equal to the three most severe transgressions: idolatry, forbidden sexual relations and bloodshed (Arakhin 15b). And moreover, the First Temple was destroyed through the sin of idolatry, forbidden sexual relations and bloodshed, whereas the Second Temple, which to this day stands in its ruin, was destroyed through the sin of baseless hatred and lashon ha-ra (Yoma 9b).

The prohibition of lashon ha-ra divides into three parts: rekhilut (tale-bearing), lashon ha-ra, and motzi shem ra (slander) (Rambam, Laws of Character Traits ch. 7). A rakhil is one who goes like a peddler (rokhel) from person to person and says: so-and-so said this about you, and such-and-such spoke thus about you. Even though his words are true, and he does not intend to harm his fellow or to disparage him, nevertheless such talk is liable to cause disputes and destroy the world. A more severe sin is lashon ha-ra: this is one who tells true things to the discredit of his fellow; that is, the prohibition in this is not that he lies, but that he publicises the disgrace of his fellow. Motzi shem ra is one who tells lies to the discredit of his fellow.

And there is a further concept in halakha, the "ba'al lashon ha-ra" (habitual speaker of evil). Almost every person sometimes stumbles in words of disparagement about his fellow, but there are people for whom this is their regular occupation in this world; they draw their joy of life from lashon ha-ra and rekhilut, about anyone at all. The Sages called them "ba'alei lashon ha-ra". And this is not merely an expression; rather, the Rambam ruled (Laws of Character Traits 7:6) that one should not live as a neighbour to a person who is a ba'al lashon ha-ra, and all the more so one should not sit with him and listen to his words.

sections.title_en: 12. The Ḥafetz Ḥayim
sections.body_en:
It is related of Rabbi Alexandri that he entered a certain city and announced that he had a remedy for whoever wants to merit long life. Many people gathered around him and asked for the wonder remedy for long life. He said to them: "Who is the man that desires life, and loves days, that he may see good? Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit" (Tehillim 34:13-14). The verse promises long life to every person who guards his tongue from speaking evil about his fellows. If you want long life, do not speak lashon ha-ra (Avoda Zara 19b; see Vayikra Rabba 16:2).

To illustrate the matter we will tell a little about one of the greatest of the generations, Rabbi Yisrael Meir of Radin. Rabbi Yisrael Meir was born more than a hundred and fifty years ago, and when he was about forty years old his heart moved him to arise and rouse the people of Israel to guarding the tongue. For this purpose he composed a long and comprehensive book on the laws of lashon ha-ra and rekhilut. He called the book "Ḥafetz Ḥayim", after the verse we mentioned, which promises long life to one who guards his tongue from speaking evil. Rabbi Yisrael Meir did not make do with composing the book alone, but would even travel and distribute it in the communities of Israel, and in his talks before his students he would speak very much about the severity of the prohibition of lashon ha-ra. After that Rabbi Yisrael Meir further managed to compose very important books, the most famous of which is the book "Mishnah Berura", a comprehensive halakhic commentary on the 'Oraḥ Ḥayim' section of the 'Shulḥan Arukh', which today is considered the most important and most studied commentary. But the first book he composed, which made his name known in the world, was "Ḥafetz Ḥayim". And today no one calls Rabbi Yisrael Meir by his name; rather, when people want to say something in his name, they say it in the name of the "Ḥafetz Ḥayim". In his personal life too the "Ḥafetz Ḥayim" was a living example of love of Israel and guarding the tongue.

The question that is asked, of course, is: at what age did the Ḥafetz Ḥayim pass away? Did he merit long life as promised? I will not weary you with details; I will only note that at the age of ninety the author of the "Ḥafetz Ḥayim" gathered his grandchildren and his students and said to them: generally it is not our custom to hold birthday parties, but I will celebrate my birthday, because in this there is publicising of the fulfilment of the promise that whoever guards his mouth and his tongue will have long life. After that he continued and lived several more years, and passed away on 24 Elul 5693 (aged ninety-seven or ninety-three). And thus the figure of the "Ḥafetz Ḥayim" has remained a symbol of the exemplary man in Torah and in love of Israel, who realised his ideas in his life and in his death.

Incidentally, because of the importance of guarding the tongue, Rav Tzvi Yehuda zt"l instituted in the "Merkaz Ha-Rav" yeshiva that every day, before the Minḥa prayer, they study the books of the "Ḥafetz Ḥayim" dealing with guarding the tongue.

sections.title_en: 13. When One Must Tell Bad Things about a Fellow
sections.body_en:
The basic rule is that in order to save a fellow from falling into a trap, it is permitted to warn him about it. For example, when Reuven wants to enter into a partnership with Shimon, and Levi, Reuven's friend, knows that there is a concern that Shimon will cheat him, because Shimon sometimes tends to cheat – if Reuven asks him about Shimon, he must tell him the truth, provided that he is very careful not to exaggerate in his words. And if it seems to him likely that Shimon is about to cheat Reuven, then even if Reuven did not come to ask his advice, Levi must come to Reuven and warn him. And this is on condition that his intention is pure, in order to save Reuven from falling into a trap, and that he is very careful not to exaggerate in his words (see on all this the Ḥafetz Ḥayim, Laws of the Prohibitions of Lashon Ha-Ra, rule 10).

And so it is written in the book Ḥafetz Ḥayim, rule 10, se'if 4: "If the people before whom he is telling (bad things about his fellow who robbed or oppressed) are able to help the one robbed and oppressed, etc., it is certainly right to do so (for through this he will save his fellow who was robbed or oppressed). And even if this benefit cannot come about through his telling, but he only intends that people should distance themselves from the way of the wicked when they hear that people condemn evildoers – and perhaps he himself will through this turn back from his evil ways and correct his deeds when he hears people condemning him for this – this too is not included in lashon ha-ra and is considered for a benefit" (and see below, halakha 23, when it is permitted to publish in a newspaper the discredit of public figures).

sections.title_en: 14. Shaming in Public
sections.body_en:
A person is forbidden to cause his fellow distress in speech, and this prohibition is called "ona'at devarim" (verbal wronging), and its source is in the verse (Vayikra 25:17): "And you shall not wrong one another; but you shall fear your God; for I am the Lord your God." For example, if suffering comes upon his fellow, he should not say to him: "Apparently you are a sinner, and therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, has punished you." But one who knows of his fellow that he is interested in hearing criticism is commanded to remark to him. And so the Sages said: "If a person sees that suffering is coming upon him, let him examine his deeds" (see Berakhot 5a-b).

And the sin of ona'at devarim is more severe than the sin of one who causes his fellow a monetary loss, for regarding ona'at devarim the Torah added and warned, "but you shall fear your God; for I am the Lord your God", which it did not warn regarding one who causes his fellow a monetary loss.

And if he whitened his fellow's face (shamed him) in public, it is as if he sheds blood: for out of great shame he first goes red and afterwards his blood withdraws from his face and he becomes pale, and his face looks like the face of a dead person. And if he is accustomed to do so, the Sages said that he has no share in the World to Come, and he goes down to Gehinnom and does not come up (Bava Metzia 58b). And of this the people of the media must be very afraid, for at times they make their living from shaming decent people in public (and it is permitted to publicise the discredit of the wicked, as we learned in the previous halakha; and see further halakha 23, when there is a need to criticise public figures in public).

And Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai said (there): "It is better for a person to throw himself into a fiery furnace than to whiten the face of his fellow in public." For so we learned from Tamar, who preferred to be burned in fire so long as she did not insult Yehuda in public (see Bereshit ch. 38), and in the end she merited that kings came from her, for the whole dynasty of the kings of the house of David is from her descendants.

But one who is wicked may be shamed in order to prevent the public from going in his ways, as it is said, "And you shall not wrong one another (amito)" – "a people (am) that is with you in Torah and mitzvot – do not wrong him" (Bava Metzia 59a; and see halakha 5, who is a wicked person).

sections.title_en: 15. The Mitzva of Loving the Convert
sections.body_en:
The mitzva "And you shall love your fellow as yourself" applies to every person of Israel, including converts; and nevertheless the Torah added a special mitzva to love the convert, as it is said (Devarim 10:19): "Love therefore the stranger (ger)."

Likewise the Torah forbade causing distress to a person of Israel, as it is said (Vayikra 25:17): "And you shall not wrong one another"; and although converts are included in the prohibition, the Torah added a special mitzva to beware of wronging the convert, as it is said (Shemot 22:20): "And a stranger shall you not wrong" (Sefer Ha-Mitzvot, positive commandment 207).

It turns out that one who loves the convert fulfils two positive commandments, and one who causes him distress transgresses two negative commandments.

The Torah's mitzva must be understood from two sides. One, that it is indeed justified to love the convert more, for he has done a great deed: he left his people and his land, and out of free choice came to join the people of Israel. And a further side is that the convert is liable to be more sensitive and vulnerable than an ordinary person, because he lacks the sense of security that a person in his natural surroundings has. And therefore there is a concern that if a person comes to speak with the convert the way he speaks with any person, he is liable inadvertently to hurt him and cause him distress. For because of his heightened sensitivity the convert is liable to interpret his words wrongly and be hurt; and because of that same sensitivity he will not even summon up the courage to settle the matter with his fellow and be reconciled. Therefore the Torah added and commanded to beware of wronging the convert, so that we weigh carefully every word and expression towards him.

sections.title_en: 16. The Mitzva of Protest
sections.body_en:
A person of Israel who sees his fellow sinning is commanded to protest against him. The protest need not stem from hatred towards the fellow but on the contrary, from love and responsibility for his situation. For just as a Jew must take care of his fellow that he should not be hungry, so he must take care that he not sin and harm his soul. And indeed we find that the mitzvot to love one's fellow and to rebuke him were said in proximity, as it is said (Vayikra 19:17-18): "You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him… but you shall love your fellow as yourself; I am the Lord." So we have learned that through rebuke true love is expressed, and in the merit of true love one rebukes.

And if he had a chance to dissuade his fellow from sinning and did not protest against him, it is considered as if he sinned himself, and he is punished for it. And the more public the sin, the greater the obligation of protest. As the Sages said (Shabbat 54b): "Whoever is able to protest against the members of his household and did not protest is held responsible for the members of his household; against the people of his city – he is held responsible for the people of his city; against the whole world – he is held responsible for the whole world" (see Peninei Halakha, The Nation and the Land 7:3).

And this is the reason for the plague that broke out in Israel after the dispute of Koraḥ and his company, a plague in which fourteen thousand seven hundred people died (Bamidbar 17:14); and had Moshe and Aharon not stopped the plague by means of the incense, who knows how many would have died.

Koraḥ and his company were a negligible minority; only a few hundred of Israel took part in the dispute, but the rest of the people stood aside and did not protest. By rights all Israel should have stood at the side of Moshe our teacher, for all the good that came to Israel in that generation came through him. And therefore it was fitting for them to drive out Koraḥ and his company in disgrace, and to say to anyone who might think of disputing with Moshe that they, the people, would not lend him their hand. But they stood aside and saw how Koraḥ and his company were shaming Moshe and Aharon, and kept silent. Not only this, but after the whole company of Koraḥ was punished by a manifest wonder, they even dared to complain about their harsh death. And since this was so, God, blessed be He, exacted payment from them for not having protested at the outset. For all those who did not protest were guilty of the death of Koraḥ and his company: had they protested against them, they would not have dared to defy Moshe, and they would not have perished.

sections.title_en: 17. The Prohibition of Flattering the Wicked
sections.body_en:
It is forbidden to flatter the wicked, as the Sages learned from the verse: "So you shall not pollute (taḥanifu) the land" (Bamidbar 35:33, and the Sifrei there). The meaning of the mitzva is that the Torah guides us not to accept the existence of wickedness in the world. When possible, we were commanded to rebuke the sinner, as it is said (Vayikra 19:17): "You shall surely rebuke your fellow"; and when it is not possible to rebuke, because only harm will grow from the rebuke, we were commanded at least not to strengthen the wicked with words of praise and flattery. For whoever flatters a wicked person strengthens him and encourages him to continue in his ways, and it turns out that he becomes a partner in strengthening evil in the world. And this is what is said (Mishlei 17:15): "He that justifies the wicked, and he that condemns the righteous, both of them alike are an abomination to the Lord." And this is what the Sages said (Sota 41b): that the punishment of one who flatters a wicked person is that he falls into Gehinnom, and even foetuses in their mothers' wombs curse him, and in the end he or his offspring will fall into the hand of that wicked person whom he strengthened with his flattery.

And even if he does not praise the evil deeds he did, but only honours him and praises his personality as a whole, he transgresses the prohibition of flattery. For even if he wants to praise a good thing he did, he is obligated to mention also his evil deeds, so that the public will not learn to go in his ways (Sha'arei Teshuva 3:189). And so it is said (Mishlei 28:4): "They that forsake the Torah praise the wicked."

And even where he is not able to protest – for example, where one is speaking of a king or a minister who will not listen to him – at least he should not flatter him, despite the unpleasantness of the matter. And so it is related in the Talmud (Sota 41) about King Agrippas, who was of gentile descent and reigned improperly. Once, when he read in the Torah at the Hakhel, he reached the verse: "You may not put a foreigner over you", and his eyes ran with tears, for he was pained because according to the Torah he is not fit to be king. The great congregation standing there was moved by Agrippas' tears, and instead of keeping silent they cheered him and said: "You are our brother, you are our brother!" "At that moment the enemies of Israel (a euphemism) became liable to destruction, because they flattered Agrippas."

And a person must be ready to lose some of his status or his money rather than flatter a person who is not worthy of honour (see Sha'arei Teshuva 3:192-193).

But in a situation of danger to life it is permitted to flatter (Tosafot Sota there). And this is what our father Ya'akov, peace be upon him, did, who said to his servants: "Thus shall you say to my lord Esav" (Bereshit 32:5). And afterwards he said to Esav: "I have seen your face as one sees the face of God, and you were pleased with me." One can explain that when a person flatters in order to protect his life, there is no concern that people will think he supports the deeds of the wicked person; rather, everyone knows that he flatters for lack of choice.

But even permitted flattery has a price. And this is what the Sages said (Sifrei Devarim 33:12): that all the tribes that took part in bowing to Esav did not merit that the Temple be built in their portion; only Binyamin, who did not bow to Esav – the Temple was built in his portion.

sections.title_en: 18. The Prohibition of Strife
sections.body_en:
The Sages said (Sanhedrin 110a): whoever persists in strife transgresses a negative commandment, as it is said (Bamidbar 17:5): "That he fare not as Koraḥ and as his company."

It is clear that all hatred between Jews is forbidden, but if one is speaking of strife the prohibition is more severe, because one is not speaking of an ordinary quarrel between people that lasts a short time, but of a fixed dedication of people to hating and fighting with their brothers.

And if the strife is directed against a decent Torah scholar, its severity is greater, because in this strife the honour of the Torah too is disgraced, and this strife causes the public to distance itself from Torah study and the fulfilment of the mitzvot. And all the more so when the strife is that of a student against his principal teacher.

And therefore the dispute of Koraḥ and his company was so severe, for it was directed against Moshe our teacher, the teacher of all Israel, who was the humblest of all men. And on this basis the Sages said (Sanhedrin 110a), and it is brought in the Shulḥan Arukh (YD 242:2): "Whoever disputes with his teacher is as one who disputes with the Shekhina. And whoever makes a quarrel with his teacher is as one who makes it with the Shekhina. And whoever complains against him is as if he complains against the Shekhina. And whoever has doubts about his teacher is as one who has doubts about the Shekhina."

However, there is positive dispute – substantive dispute without personal hatred, like the dispute of Shammai and Hillel. Out of such a dispute matters are clarified and refined, and therefore it has value; and about it the Sages said (Avot 5:17) that it will in the end endure, that is, both views that were clarified out of the dispute will endure. But a dispute that is not for the sake of Heaven will not in the end endure, and all who take part in the dispute perish from the world, like Koraḥ and his company.

sections.title_en: 19. Dispute against the Wicked
sections.body_en:
Peace and unity express in a tangible way faith in the one God. And especially the people of Israel, which was created in order to reveal the word of God in the world, must be in unity: just as God is one, so the people of Israel must be one. Therefore when the people of Israel is in unity, its greatness is revealed and its enemies fall before it; and when it is not in unity, it falls before its enemies (see Peninei Halakha, "The Nation and the Land" 2:5).

But when one is speaking of the wicked, who have separated themselves from God and from His people, and from the good traits that are the expression of cleaving to God, the dispute against them does not create division. For they themselves have decided to separate from the universal unity, and therefore one must dispute with them, because through the dispute against them one separates the disintegrating element and prevents it from continuing to cause damage. And as explained in 'Sha'arei Teshuva' (3:59), had the sons of Binyamin gone out against the men of Giv'a who abused the concubine, they would not afterwards have fallen in the war against the other tribes of Israel.

And one who refrains from protesting and standing against the wicked on the pretext that he does not want to make a dispute is punished for their transgressions. For whoever does not protest and separate himself from deeds of wickedness and injustice becomes a partner to them and transgresses a negative commandment (as explained above, halakhot 16-17). At times self-sacrifice is required for this, as it was after the sin of the Golden Calf, when the sons of Levi gathered to Moshe and by the word of God killed the sinners, and as Pineḥas son of Elazar the Kohen did against the prince of the tribe of Shimon (Sha'arei Teshuva 3:59).

The people of truth are those who stand with courage against wickedness, and take care not to dispute with good people. And those whose fear of Heaven is counterfeit exploit the prohibition of strife in order to flatter wicked people with status, but find all kinds of justifications to make a dispute "for the sake of Heaven" against good and upright people who are weaker than them.

sections.title_en: 20. One Compels against the Trait of Sedom
sections.body_en:
The Sages said: "One compels against the trait of Sedom." That is, one compels a person not to behave according to the custom of the people of Sedom. And what is the trait of the people of Sedom? That they do not want to let others benefit. And even where another person's benefit causes them no harm at all, but rather "this one benefits and that one loses nothing" (Bava Kamma 20b), nevertheless, out of the evil of their heart, they do not want to let others benefit. And about this the Sages said: "One compels against the trait of Sedom", that is, one obligates a person to let others benefit from things that belong to him, when he has no loss from it.

The people of Sedom did not want to let others benefit from their land and their property. And although they had a good land, like the garden of the Lord, full of every good thing, and they were very rich, and had wayfarers and poor people passed through their land they would have lost nothing, they did not want poor people to come and live among them, so that they would not benefit from their good land.

And so they said in the mishna in Avot (5:10): "One who says, 'What is mine is mine and what is yours is yours' – this is an average trait. And some say this is the trait of Sedom." And there is no dispute here; rather the commentators explained that indeed one who says "what is mine is mine and what is yours is yours" does not yet sin with the trait of Sedom, because there is not yet in this an expression of his begrudging his fellow benefit from his property. Nevertheless, through such a position one is close to reaching the trait of Sedom, for in essence his main intention is that he should not need to give anything to his fellow (R. Ovadya of Bartenura; and the Rashbatz in his commentary Magen Avot).

An example for halakha: when brothers come to divide fields that their father bequeathed them, and one of them has a field beside one of the father's fields – if all the fields are of equal value, the brother can ask to inherit the field adjacent to his field, so that his holding will be continuous and he will not need to trouble himself to go between his fields. And if his brothers, out of pettiness, are not willing to give him the adjacent field, according to most poskim one compels them to give him the field adjacent to his field: since they lose nothing by it, they are not allowed to behave according to the trait of the people of Sedom (Bava Batra 12b; SA ḤM 174:1).

sections.title_en: 21. Whether to "Inform" on Someone Who Broke a Window
sections.body_en:
Question: My friend broke an expensive window in one of the public buildings in the settlement. He did not plan to break the window; rather, he was being somewhat rowdy and throwing stones, and unintentionally one stone hit the window. There is a sort of tacit agreement that in order to protect the friend who broke the window, all the boys who know about it will keep silent, and even if they are asked they will not inform on the one who broke it. In the eyes of the friends, whoever tells is considered a betrayer of trust and one who sins with lashon ha-ra. Must we report to those responsible in the settlement who broke the window, or refrain from doing so?

Answer: The one who broke the window is obligated to pay for the damage. And if he does not come of his own accord to pay, you must try to rebuke him and explain to him that whoever damages his fellow's property, and all the more so public property, is obligated to pay for the damage. And if he is not willing to accept responsibility for it, you must inform those responsible for public property that so-and-so broke the window, so that they can collect from him the payment for the repair.

And this is a Torah mitzva, as the Sages learned (Sifra, Kedoshim): whoever knows testimony that can save his fellow's money is obligated to testify about it and not keep silent, as it is said (Vayikra 19:16): "Neither shall you stand idly by the blood of your fellow." That is, one must save not only the life of one's fellow but also his money. And so the Rambam wrote in Sefer Ha-Mitzvot (negative commandment 297), and so it is written in Sefer Ha-Ḥinukh (mitzva 237). And there is in this also a further mitzva, that of returning a lost object. And since it is a mitzva to save one's fellow's money, there is no prohibition of lashon ha-ra here (Ḥafetz Ḥayim, Lashon Ha-Ra 10:1, and Rekhilut 9:3).

As a rule one must know that the prohibition of lashon ha-ra was intended to prevent distress to an ordinary person, and not to serve as a shield and refuge for criminals and those who cause damage. On the contrary, one must struggle against one who causes damage and does not pay, and do everything so that he will correct what he did. Therefore, if you have the strength to stand firm with courage, you should announce that if the one who broke the window does not admit it himself, you will go and tell that he broke the window. And if you do not have the strength to stand against them and tell them what must be done, at any rate do not stand aside, seeing public property damaged and keeping silent; rather, turn to those responsible and tell them who broke the window, so that they can do justice.

In general one must be careful not to use the Torah and its mitzvot according to the need of the hour. All year round there are boys who enjoy telling lashon ha-ra about friends and teachers, and suddenly, when there is a need to tell the truth, they wrap themselves in self-righteousness and refrain from telling for reasons of "lashon ha-ra". Sometimes boys are ready to laugh at anyone who does not belong to their group, abuse the weak, laugh at other groups, rejoice at their misfortune; and only when one of them has to stand trial and pay for his deeds do they suddenly remember all the stringencies of the prohibition of lashon ha-ra.[2]

notes_en.en: And so wrote Rabbi Yisrael Isser, one of the great rabbis of Vilna, in his book Pitḥei Teshuva on Oraḥ Ḥayim (Vilna 5635, siman 156, quoted from Responsa Yeḥaveh Da'at 4:60), who wrote: "Behold, the Magen Avraham and likewise the books of mussar expanded on the severity of the prohibition of lashon ha-ra, and I have seen fit to point out the other side: that there is a greater sin than this, and it too is very common, namely one who holds himself back from informing his fellow where there is a need to save the oppressed from the hand of his oppressor, because he is concerned about the prohibition of lashon ha-ra. For example, one who sees someone lying in wait for his fellow to kill him by cunning, or digging a tunnel in the dead of night and darkness into the house or shop of his fellow, and holds himself back from informing his fellow and warning him in good time, because he thinks that it is included in the prohibition of lashon ha-ra. And in truth one who behaves thus, his sin is too great to bear, and he transgresses 'Neither shall you stand idly by the blood of your fellow'. And the same applies to money matters: for what difference is there between digging a tunnel and seeing his fellow's servants stealing from him, or his partner stealing from his business, or his fellow misleading him and overcharging him in buying and selling, or that in his innocence he is lending money to a person who is a wicked borrower and will not pay? And the Sages already said (Bava Kamma 119a): whoever robs his fellow of a peruta is as if he takes his soul from him, etc. And so the Rambam ruled (Robbery and Lost Property 1:13). And likewise in matters of matchmaking, where the young man is a bad and worthless person and a swindler, or he is sickly, and he seeks to marry, etc. – all these are included in the mitzva of returning a lost object, the loss of his body or the loss of his money, as they said in Sanhedrin (73a). And the matter is given over to the heart: if the intention of the one telling his fellow is bad, this is included in the prohibition of lashon ha-ra; but if his intention is for good, to warn his fellow and save him from a snare, it is a great mitzva, and blessing will come upon him."

sections.title_en: 22. Whether to Run Away with the Class
sections.body_en:
Question: A group of girls from my class decided that it would be very amusing to disappear suddenly from the high school before the last lesson. The teacher will come and find the class empty and will not understand what is happening, and it will be very funny. But for the move to succeed, all the girls must cooperate as one, for then they will not be able to punish all the girls of the class. But if some run away and some do not, it will not succeed, and it is even possible that those who ran away will be punished. The question is whether I, who do not want to take part in this prank, must run away with everyone so as not to harm the unity of the class, or whether it is better to stay, even though they may laugh at me and perhaps even distance themselves from my company.

Answer: This prank is forbidden because it insults the teacher, and as is known it is forbidden to insult and cause distress to a person (see above, halakha 14). And all the more so it is forbidden to insult a teacher who teaches you Torah or wisdom. And there is nothing more insulting than a whole class that disappears. This is truly included in shaming a person in public. And indeed, according to the plan not one of the girls will remain in the class to see her in her embarrassment; nevertheless, how will she face the teaching staff, and how will she come to class the next day, when everyone knows that they ran away from her lesson? Imagine what sad thoughts may flood her: not only is one girl unhappy with the lesson, but all of them. Perhaps she is a failure; perhaps she erred in choosing her profession. You do not know what difficulties she is coping with in her life, and who knows what further insult might cause. Perhaps her livelihood is tight, and only yesterday the principal informed her that it is not clear whether she will be able to continue teaching next year; and now that the whole class has disappeared, the principal will certainly think she is a bad teacher and will dismiss her. And perhaps just a month ago her husband was also dismissed, and how will they manage without a salary, when they have to buy food and pay a mortgage and tuition for their son at the yeshiva high school (1,200 shekels a month) and for their daughter at the ulpana (another 1,200 shekels a month)?

The Sages said (Avot 3:11): "One who whitens the face of his fellow in public… even though he has Torah and good deeds to his credit, has no share in the World to Come." The Sages further said (Yalkut Shimoni, Vayeshev, remez 145): "One who whitens the face of his fellow in public is as if he sheds his blood." And indeed it seemingly appears that the Sages exaggerated in their words: would a person, for one time that he shames his fellow, lose his share in the World to Come? And is shaming like bloodshed? After an insult a person generally recovers, whereas one who has been killed will no longer recover.

But if we look into their words, we find that they are aimed at the truth. For indeed it sometimes happens that a person causes his fellow such an insult that his whole life from then on will be different. If, for example, following the class's wish to make fun at the teacher's expense, the teacher loses her job, and this causes a crisis in her marriage, then indeed the insult they caused her will be close in severity to bloodshed, and the punishment in the world of truth will be very severe, to the point that those who shamed her will have almost no share in the World to Come. And indeed many times the insult is not so severe, but only a slight distress that leaves no scar on the soul. But the Sages expressed themselves severely against one who shames his fellow, so that people would know how far things can go.

And if we are precise in the language of the Sages, we find that they did not say that the one who shames has lost all of his World to Come, but that he has lost a share – it may be that he lost a large share, and it may be a small share. And likewise one who shames his fellow is as if he sheds his blood: it may be that he shed a little of his blood, in that he went pale from shame, and it may be that he shed much of his blood. That is, each case is judged on its own. Generally, one who shames his fellow transgresses a prohibition that is relatively light compared to one who sheds blood, but sometimes it is possible that he approaches the severity of one who sheds blood.

In any event, even if the teacher's situation is good, it is forbidden to hurt her, and it is forbidden to harm the honour of learning.

And there is no place for the claim that if you stay in the class you will harm the social cohesion. For social cohesion is good as long as it strengthens the positive foundations in the girls. But when cohesion is exploited for bad, it is reprehensible. Generally in such cohesion a number of girls take control of the class and stifle the voice of the rest. Therefore, be courageous and do not give in. Be true to the good in you and do not surrender. Tell everyone that you are staying in the class, and try to persuade as many girls as possible to stay with you (see above, halakha 16).

The end of the story was that that girl succeeded in organising a group that announced it would not run away. The prank was cancelled. Subsequently the class came together around more positive values.

sections.title_en: 23. Whether It Is Permitted to Publish in a Newspaper the Discredit of Public Figures
sections.body_en:
Question: Is it permitted to publish in a newspaper things to the discredit of public figures? Is there not in this the prohibition of lashon ha-ra, and of shaming a person in public?

Answer: When there is a public figure who does a bad deed that causes harm to the public, one must sound the alarm about it, in order to prevent the harm that is liable to come from him to the public. Before taking pity on his honour, one must take pity on the public that is liable to be harmed by his bad deeds. And so the prophets of Israel behaved, who would rebuke the kings for their bad deeds. At first one must try to rebuke privately; but when private rebuke does not help, one must criticise and denounce the bad deeds publicly. And especially in a democratic government, in which the public chooses its representatives, there is great benefit in the public knowing the opinions and deeds of its elected officials, so that it can decide whom to choose. And one who is able to publish the bad deeds of one of the elected officials and does not publish them transgresses the prohibition "Neither shall you stand idly by the blood of your fellow", as explained above (halakha 21). And since there is benefit to the public in this, there is no prohibition of lashon ha-ra in it, as we have learned (above, halakhot 13 and 21).

However, one must be very careful to follow the rules we learned in the mitzva "In righteousness shall you judge your fellow" (Vayikra 19:15; above, halakha 9). For if one is speaking of a righteous person, then even when the deed he did appears bad, if it is possible to explain it by some logical explanation in a positive way, it is a mitzva to judge him favourably. And if there is no way to judge him favourably, and it is clear that he is doing bad deeds, and private rebuke does not help, one must criticise him in public, since his deeds have public implications. But one must point out that as a rule this person is not considered bad; only for these deeds one must criticise him.

When one is speaking of an average person, if it is possible to judge the deeds he did favourably and unfavourably equally, it is a mitzva to judge him favourably. But when after careful examination it appears that his deeds are bad, there is no need to judge him favourably, and one must denounce his deeds.

And if he is a wicked person, then even when his deeds are average, and they can be judged favourably and unfavourably to an equal degree, one must judge him unfavourably.

In addition, when one is speaking of a wicked person whom there are people liable to err and follow in his ways, then even when he is not in a public position, as long as he has public influence and there are people who are drawn after his bad opinions and deeds, it is a mitzva to tell of his discredit (Sha'arei Teshuva 3:218). And so the Sages said (Tanḥuma, Pineḥas 2): "Just as the Holy One, blessed be He, busies Himself with the praise of the righteous to publicise them in the world, so He busies Himself with the discredit of the wicked to publicise them in the world. He publicised Pineḥas for praise and publicised Zimri for disgrace; about them it is said (Mishlei 10:7): 'The memory of the righteous shall be for a blessing, but the name of the wicked shall rot.'"

Without the righteous denouncing the wicked, they have no ability to defeat the wicked. According to logic, seemingly every struggle between a righteous person and a wicked one should end in the victory of the wicked. For the righteous person has all kinds of moral restraints: he cannot lie; if rules for the battle are set he cannot break them. And thus the wicked person will always have an advantage: he can spread lies about his opponent, he can break the rules when it benefits him, and thus he will always win.

But the righteous person has one advantage, the moral advantage: he can define the wicked person as wicked. And since values carry weight, the determination that so-and-so is wicked will cause his weakening among his supporters and the strengthening of his opponents. And thus, even if the righteous act according to the rules of morality, they will win. But if the righteous give up their main right – to define the wicked as wicked and to denounce them before the sun – they no longer have a chance to win.

May it be His will that courageous righteous people arise who, out of immense love for the people of Israel and for each and every Jew, will stand against the wicked to denounce them, and will save Israel with love and compassion. And out of this the wicked too will repent, and all will recognise and know that the kingship is the Lord's, and through cleaving to His Torah the complete rectification will come to the world.
